concept.name: Net exposure
concept.definition: The difference between a portfolio's long and short exposures, expressed as a percentage of capital: long exposure minus short exposure. It measures net directional sensitivity to broad market moves.
concept.intuition: It is the portfolio's lean: net long books gain when markets rise, net short books gain when they fall, and zero net is directionally market-neutral.
concept.mechanics: Subtract total short market value from total long market value and divide by net asset value. Managers adjust net exposure with their outlook; it is the first-order determinant of how the fund responds to a market-wide move, though it hides leverage, which gross exposure reveals.
concept.formula: Net exposure = (|long positions| - |short positions|) / net asset value * 100%.
concept.failure_modes: Net exposure assumes longs and shorts respond to 'the market' symmetrically; when they decouple — crowded shorts squeezing while longs fall — a low-net book can still bleed heavily. It ignores factor, sector, and beta mismatches between the legs.
concept.misconceptions: Net zero exposure is not zero risk: it is only first-order directional neutrality, and leverage, factor tilts, and basis between the long and short legs remain fully exposed.
concept.example: A fund 60% long and 40% short has 100% gross and 20% net exposure: it participates in market direction at about one-fifth weight while carrying a full book of positions.
